workEn: The Secret History of the Mongols
title: 元朝秘史 §§267–270
titleEn: The Secret History of the Mongols — §§267–270: The fall of the Tangut, Ögödei's accession and the western campaigns
part: §§267–270 — The fall of the Tangut, Ögödei's accession and the western campaigns
source: Mongγol-un niγuča tobčiyan (The Secret History of the Mongols), §§267–270, in the Ming Chinese-character phonetic transcription, as edited with a romanized reading by Shiratori Kurakichi 白鳥庫吉, 音訳蒙文元朝秘史 (Tokyo, 1943), itself based on the Ye Dehui 葉德輝 printed edition of 1905/1908; text taken from the Japanese Wikisource transcription, archived and verified against it character for character. Shiratori died in 1942, so the edition was public domain in Japan before the URAA date and was never restored in the United States. Section numbering (§) is the standard citation system. Romanization convention: Shiratori's, kept exactly as he prints it (γ, ġ, ṅ, ž, č, and the raised dot of γ̇). Translations are made fresh from the Mongolian, with the Ming interlinear Chinese glosses as the primary crib. No modern translation was consulted. langCode is null: there is no text-to-speech for Middle Mongol.
about: Chinggis takes Dörmegei and receives Burqan's homage, but is revolted by it; he has the Tangut ruler put to death, shares out the spoils, and decrees that the Tangut be wiped out. In the Pig year he goes up to Heaven. In the Rat year the princes gather at Köde'ü-Aral and raise Ögödei Qan, and Cha'adai and Tolui hand over the guard and the central people. Ögödei sends armies against Sultan Qaliba and, under Sübegetei, as far as the Adil-Jajaq river, appoints Batu and Güjüg as elders of the princes, and rules that each prince send his eldest son on campaign. A note on the text: the Mongol is a Ming Chinese-character transcription, and the glosses in square brackets are the Ming glossators' own; where the English departs from them or is unsure, the note says so.
draftNote: The Mongol readings follow Shiratori throughout; the English is a first drafting.

sentences.i: “Having given Iluqu-Burqan the name Shidurqu, and Iluqu-Burqan Shidurqu having been come to, Chinggis Qahan said there, ‘Let Iluqu be put to death,’ and said,
sentences.n: The quotation opens here and runs to nögčiġetügei in the next unit. It speaks of Chinggis in the third person, which is odd inside his own decree, and the clause iregdežü (the passive of ire- “come”, Ming 被來着, “being come”) with Šidurqu-ji in the accusative does not parse cleanly, so the middle of this unit is my best reading, not a sure one. Nögčijefkün is printed with an f, but the Han is 惕坤 (t + kün), so f is a slip for t and the ending is -tkün, taken as one ending like -dkün / -dqun; the Ming 敎過去者 means “let (him) be made to pass away”, a euphemism, so “put to death”. Two keġen “saying” stand in the decree; I give them as “said”.

sentences.n: Ideġe ideküi žaγ̇ura is “while the food is eaten” (Ming 茶飯 喫的 間), so the command is to say the curse at every meal. sentences.n: Keġen žarliγ bolba again closes the decree, as at the end of §267.

sentences.n: Altan amin is “golden life” (Ming 金 性命 守), altan here being the adjective “golden, precious”, not the Jin emperor. Sakin “guarding” is saki- + the converb -n, aγsad “those who were” (Ming 有的每). The next four units are one long list of what was handed over, and I split it for reading.

sentences.n: Kebteġül “night guard” (Ming 宿衞), qorčin “quiver-bearers” (帶弓箭的), naiman miṅγad “eight thousand” and turγaγ̇ud “day guards” (Ming 散班每) follow the house renderings of §§224–236.

sentences.n: Čaγ̇ada is “at the side, near” (Ming 親近, “near, close”). Qān ečige-jin is “of Father Qan”, i.e. Chinggis, and min-u “my” follows, which is odd: the voice has slipped to Ögödei’s (or the chronicler’s) “my person” from the narrative. sentences.n: Qorči-jin is “of the quiver-bearer” (Ming 帶弓箭的 的); gežige is “reserve, rear support” (Ming 後援). Qojar-i “the two (object)” and the causative ajalaγ̇ulba “had (them) campaign” give “sent out”. sentences.n: Basa “again” and urida “formerly, first” (Ming 再, 先), then Sübeġetei baγ̇atur-i, Sübegetei with his title “hero, brave warrior” (Ming 勇士) and the accusative. sentences.n: Shiratori prints no opening mark for this decree, so the opening quotation mark in `i` is mine; the closing mark is at the last ajalaγ̇ultuγai, in the unit at words 414–421. Ajalaγ̇ultuγai is “let (him) cause to campaign”, and modekün is mede- “know, manage” + -kün, printed with o (Ming 管的每). Köġüd-ü-ġen is “their own sons” (a linking -ü- before the reflexive after the plural). Jeke köġü is “great son”, the eldest; kü is the particle “indeed”. I take Ögödei still to be speaking, and the next stretch to be Cha’adai’s own words, reported inside his: ügüležü is “speaking” (Ming 說着), irerün “as he comes” (Ming 來). Keġežü irežüġüi is “saying, came”; the subject is not named, and I take it as Cha’adai arriving with the words: it answers ügüležü irerün at the start of his speech, as the frame “X ügülerün: … keġen” does.
